title: Parental Bonding and the Recognition and Preference for One's Own Child's Body Odour
abstract: Previous research has shown that parents can recognise and positively evaluate their infant's odour, but the extent to which these processes relate to individual differences in bonding remains unclear. Addressing this gap, we examined whether parent-reported bonding difficulties are associated with odour recognition accuracy and hedonic evaluation of a child's body odour. A sample of 86 parent–child dyads (children aged 3 months to 3 years) participated in a body odour assessment paradigm. Bonding was measured using the Postpartum Bonding Questionnaire (PBQ). Odour identification involved selecting the child's odour from six samples, including the child's own odour, four odours from other children and a blank sample. Pleasantness was rated for each sample on a visual analogue scale ranging from 0 to 100. Logistic and linear regression analyses were conducted, controlling for parent sex, parent age and child age. Higher PBQ scores, indicating greater parent-reported bonding difficulties, were associated with a higher likelihood of correctly identifying the child's odour, and this effect remained significant after controlling for other covariates. In contrast, bonding difficulties were not associated with the child's body odour pleasantness ratings. These findings suggest that parental olfactory processing comprises at least two partially dissociable components: offspring recognition and hedonic evaluation, which may serve distinct functions in parent–child relationships.
